'''''Cephalocereus polylophus''''' is a [[species]] of [[cactus]] [[Endemism|endemic]] to Mexico.<ref name=POWO_52188-2/> Often grown under the [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Neobuxbaumia polylopha''''', it is popular with cactus growers and reproduces well in cultivation.<ref name=Yet07/> 

==Description==
''Cephalocereus polylophus'' grows individually and reaches heights of up to {{cvt|13|m|ft|0}} or even {{cvt|15|m|ft|0}} and can grow to weigh many tons.<ref name=Yet07/> The columnar shoots are initially light green and become darker with age. They have diameters of up to {{cvt|50|cm|ftin|0}}. The 22 to 36 (rarely from 10) narrow, slightly curved ribs are separated from each other by a sharp furrow. The single, flexible central spine, which can also be missing, is often shorter than the seven to eight marginal spines. The marginal spines are flexible and {{cvt|1|to|2|cm|in|1}} long. They are yellowish to brownish and turn gray with age.<ref name="Anderson Eggli 2005 p. 439"/>

The flowers usually appear in groups near the tips of the shoots. They are dark red, {{cvt|4|to|6|cm|in|1}} long and reach a diameter of {{cvt|30|to|35|mm|in|1}}. Its pericarpel and floral tube are covered with fairly large tubercles and small scales that are glabrous in the axillae. The egg-shaped, green fruits are {{cvt|24|to|40|mm|in|1}} long and covered with scales, wool and bristles.<ref name="Anderson Eggli 2005 p. 439"/> The fruits are edible by humans and have a delicate, nutty flavor.<ref name=Yet07/>

==Taxonomy==
The first description as ''Cereus polylophus'' was published in 1828 by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]].<ref name=POWO_52188-2/><ref name=DeCan28>{{cite book |last=de Candolle |first=A.P. |contribution=Cereus |title=Mémoires du Muséum d'histoire naturelle |publisher=G. Dufour |volume=17 |date=1828 |contribution-url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/26229182 |access-date=2023-11-05}}</ref> The specific epithet ''polylophus'' is derived from the Greek words ''poly'' for 'many' and ''lophos'' for 'crest',<ref name=LiddScot40>{{Cite book |last1=Liddell |last2=Scott |date=1940 |contribution=λόφος |title=A Greek–English Lexicon |publication-place=Oxford |publisher=Clarendon Press |contribution-url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0057:entry=lo/fos |access-date=2023-11-06 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref> referring to the numerous ribs of the species. [[Nathaniel Lord Britton]] and [[Joseph Nelson Rose]] placed the species in the genus ''Cephalocereus'' in 1909. Further [[Synonym (taxonomy)|nomenclature synonyms]] are ''Pilocereus polylophus'', ''Neobuxbaumia polylopha'', and ''Carnegiea polylopha''.<ref name=POWO_52188-2/>

==Distribution==
''Cephalocereus polylophus'' is native to the Mexican states of Hidalgo, Querétaro, Guanajuato and San Luis Potosí.<ref name="On-line Guide to the positive identification of Members of the Cactus Family y332">{{cite web | title=On-line Guide to the positive identification of Members of the Cactus Family | website=On-line Guide to the positive identification of Members of the Cactus Family | url=https://cactiguide.com/cactus/?genus=neobuxbaumia&species=polylopha | access-date=2023-11-05}}</ref>

==Conservation==
''Neobuxbaumia polylopha'' was assessed as "[[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]]" in the 2009 [[IUCN Red List]], where it is said to be native only to the Mexican states of Hidalgo, Querétaro and Guanajuato.<ref name=IUCN/> {{As of|2023|April}}, ''N. polylopha'' was regarded as a synonym of ''Cephalocereus polylophus'', which [[Plants of the World Online]] gives a somewhat wider distribution.<ref name=POWO_52188-2/>
